title: Phacelia as a green manure
subtitle: A fast-growing annual that feeds bees and improves soil in six weeks.
excerpt: Phacelia is one of the best green manures for the UK kitchen garden. It grows fast from spring to autumn, fixes bare soil, feeds pollinators with lavender-blue flowers, and breaks down quickly when cut and left on the surface.
sourceNotes: Green manure performance data from Garden Organic trials (gardensorganic.org.uk). Bee-forage value from research by the Bumblebee Conservation Trust. Frost tolerance threshold widely cited in UK horticultural literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fast-growing crop sown to cover bare soil and then cut and left on the surface or incorporated into the bed to add organic matter and nutrients. Phacelia, field beans, mustard, and clover are common green manures.

content.text: Phacelia is a fast-growing annual grown as a

to cover bare soil between crops or at the end of the season. Sow it on any open bed and within six to eight weeks the ground is covered, weeds are suppressed, and bees are arriving in numbers. Cut it before it sets seed and leave it on the surface to break down.

It germinates at soil temperatures from around 8 degrees Celsius upwards. In the UK, this means sowing from late March. Sow again in August and September to cover ground after summer crops are cleared.
Rake the soil roughly level. Broadcast the seed thinly across the bed and rake in lightly. No need for precise spacing. Germination takes five to ten days in warm weather. Water if dry.

A late sowing in September will cover the ground into October and November. Phacelia is killed by hard frosts (below about minus 5 degrees Celsius), so autumn-sown plants collapse in winter and the dead matter rots down over winter without any cutting needed.

Cut phacelia before the flowers open if you want the nitrogen to stay in the green matter rather than going to seed. Leave it to flower if bee-forage is the priority: the lavender-blue flowers are a reliable bee plant and the forage benefit lasts two to three weeks.

Cut the plants to the ground with shears or a scythe and leave all the material on the surface as a mulch. In warm weather it breaks down in two to four weeks. In autumn, it takes longer. Do not leave it in large clumps: spread it evenly so it dries out rather than sitting in a mat and fostering slugs.

attrs.title: Phacelia and succession sowing
attrs.body: Sow phacelia on any bed that will not be replanted for six weeks. It works well after early potatoes are lifted in July, after the last asparagus cut in June, and on any brassica bed that will not be planted until spring. A succession of short sowings throughout the season covers ground and keeps the bee forage coming through summer.

items.cause: Soil too cold (below 8 degrees Celsius) or too dry.
items.fix: Sow later in the season when soil has warmed. Water in after sowing in dry weather.

items.symptom: Phacelia flowered and set seed before I could cut it
items.cause: Fast growth in warm summer conditions.
items.fix: Cut as soon as flowers appear rather than waiting. Phacelia can run to seed in four to five weeks in hot July weather. If seed has already set, cut and remove the seed heads before they drop.

items.symptom: Slugs under the cut phacelia mat
items.cause: A thick, damp layer of wilting plants is good slug habitat.
items.fix: Spread the cut material thinly so it dries quickly. Avoid cutting just before heavy rain if slug pressure is high.
